alignments.note: Imperative with its English subject pronoun under rule 17; the *ye* stands immediately after the verb, which rule 36 makes the imperative's rather than a vocative's.
Short divine name rendered *Jehovah*. The margin's Hallelujah gloss is read and set aside under rule 38.

Predicate adjective of the verbless clause takes the construction-supplied copula under rule 20; the anticipatory *it* standing before it is placed separately, since the Hebrew writes an infinitive subject for this predicate.

The Hebrew's subject of `טוֹב` is the infinitive phrase `זַמְּרָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ`, which the ASV extraposes and renders in full, putting an anticipatory *it* where that subject would stand. Rule 25's extraposition sentence governs: the pronoun denotes nothing the verse names and is its own `added` unit, exactly as `תוֹעֲבַת כְּסִילִים סוּר מֵרָע` → *it is an abomination to fools to depart from evil*. The competing reading keeps *it is* whole on `טוֹב` under rule 20's leading example *that it was good*; I took the split because that example has no extraposed clausal subject, its *it* denoting a referent the verse names.

Bare infinitive construct with no preposition takes the English infinitive marker under rule 52's closing sentence; *praises* carries the verb's own lexeme and joins its one rendering under rule 44, and the *unto* is the preposition the English verb's valency needs to reach its bare object `אֱלֹהֵינוּ`. Head on the lexical verb.
Construct noun keeps only its own word.
Pronominal suffix as possessive under rule 18.

The third colon writes no subject for `נָעִים`, and the ASV coordinates `נָאוָה תְהִלָּה` as a clause of its own rather than extraposing it, so nothing is anticipated here: the supplied *it is* is rule 20's construction-supplied copula joining the predicate adjective, as in that rule's own *that it was good*.
Subject noun of the third colon.
Predicate adjective with the construction-supplied copula under rule 20; the subject noun `תְהִלָּה` keeps its own word.

No conjunction morpheme stands between the two predicates of the third line; the coordinating *and* answers to nothing and is `added` under rule 14's closing sentences. The ASV italic corroborates it, by rule 7.

review_notes: Corrected: the *it* of *it is good* is the anticipatory subject of an extraposed infinitive clause the Hebrew writes (`זַמְּרָה אֱלֹהֵינוּ`), so rule 25's extraposition sentence makes it `added` and leaves *is good* on `טוֹב`. The third colon is left as accepted, because there the ASV coordinates `נָאוָה תְהִלָּה` as its own clause and extraposes nothing, so rule 20's construction-supplied *it is* stands with `נָעִים`.
The alternative rendering in the margin (*Or, For he is good ... For he is gracious*) was read and set aside; the printed text governs, by rule 38.
